knowledge.question: Is it easier to get high prices on cheap items or expensive items?
knowledge.answer: Cheap items. Levi gets over retail on low-ticket items, like little $10 retail pieces, because buyers don't have time to look up reviews or market value in an auction. On a $600 item, you'll rarely get over retail because it depends on how many viewers want it and have $300 to spend that day. Focus on both your per-unit price and the percentage of retail you paid; profit is made on buy cost and sale price.

knowledge.question: Are resellers bad for my show?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi enjoys having resellers because they drive prices up when they compete with consumers. A consumer will pay up to about 50% of retail, while a reseller is more careful. His example: a $75 Lego bag that a reseller would pay $20 for, but a consumer will pay $30. Buyers also pay more for brands like Champion.

knowledge.question: Should I pull out my best items to sell elsewhere?
knowledge.answer: No. Like a good bin store owner, leave the good stuff in and let buyers get a bargain so they come back and spend more. Levi sold a Canon camera he could have sold for $1,000 on eBay with a $450 start; it went for $550, the buyer made $500 profit, and he keeps coming back and bidding on more. Keep your customers happy and they keep buying.

knowledge.question: Do seasonal items still sell out of season?
knowledge.answer: Yes, don't limit yourself. Levi sells Speedo floaties for about $8 on average in December because buyers would pay $30 in store in summer. Essentials like Dove soap and skincare sell well too; some buyers stock up for a year or two. He once sold 100 Dove soaps in a row at $5.

knowledge.question: What are the Whatnot shipping tiers by weight?
knowledge.answer: Levi breaks it down: First Class covers 0 to 3 ounces, under one pound is ground shipping, and once it hits 16 ounces it's Priority Mail, which covers 1 to 5 lbs for $9.21. Over five pounds (even 80.1 ounces) automatically becomes ground shipping unless you change it in shipping settings, which he doesn't recommend for beginners because it scares buyers away. Under one pound is cheaper than $9.21; the lowest he's seen for 4 to 7 ounces is about $4.50, with separate ranges for 8 to 11 and 12 to 15 ounces.

knowledge.question: Why is the large flat rate box such a good deal on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: A large flat rate box ships up to 70 pounds for $9.21, the same price as 1 to 5 lbs Priority Mail. Levi calls it very undervalued: you could throw 100 batteries in it at 60 pounds and the customer still pays $9.21. Just remember a large flat rate label can only go on an actual USPS large flat rate box.

knowledge.question: How do I create a custom shipping profile that caps bundles at 10 items?
knowledge.answer: Divide 80 ounces (the 5 lb limit) by your max bundle: 80 / 10 = 8 ounces. On desktop go to Seller Hub, then Shipping Settings, then Shipping Profiles, create a profile (name it anything), enter 8 ounces and set a maximum of 10 items. That keeps every bundle at or under 80 ounces so it's always Priority Mail, and at the end of the show you can toggle the labels to a large flat rate box since it's the same price.

knowledge.question: Why use a standard weight profile instead of weighing every item?
knowledge.answer: Levi says time is money on Whatnot, so you want to avoid weighing each individual item. Big sellers move with speed because they know their average weight (8 ounces in his beauty show) and that 10 of their items fit in a large flat rate box, so the actual weight doesn't matter once they switch the label to flat rate.

knowledge.question: Why set my electronics shipping profile to 15 ounces instead of 16?
knowledge.answer: Levi's electronics bundle is five items, and 80 / 5 = 16 ounces, but he sets the profile to 15 ounces with a max bundle of five. At 16 ounces a new buyer sees $9.21 shipping on their first item and runs away thinking your shipping is expensive. At 15 ounces the first item stays in cheaper ground shipping, and once they buy a second item they're automatically in Priority Mail at a max of $9.21.

knowledge.question: How does 'free shipping after two items' actually work on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Whatnot charges shipping expecting one item, so the first item might be around $6.20 depending on where the buyer is, the second maybe $3 or $4, and it adds up to a max of $9.21. After that, the buyer's screen shows free shipping on the remaining items in the bundle (items 3–5 in his electronics show, items 3–10 in his beauty show). Buyers get encouraged to grab that second item because they know they're close to free shipping.

knowledge.question: Can I change the weight on a label after the show?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says even if a box only weighs 2 or 2.5 pounds, you can go into your shipments and change the weight up to 80 ounces and it'll still be $9.21. It doesn't hurt your shipping or the buyer's, because they paid $9.21 for the 1 to 5 lb range, and it lets you use free USPS Priority Mail boxes.

knowledge.question: How can bundle shipping help me get more sales as a beginner?
knowledge.answer: There are so many new buyers on the app who don't understand that after two items the rest ship free, and they're afraid of shipping costs. Levi says to ask your viewers next stream how many joined the app today; you'll get at least two or three. Explaining bundle shipping to them is a big selling point most sellers miss.

knowledge.question: What box sizes am I allowed to use for a Priority Mail bundle?
knowledge.answer: Levi says buyers pay for up to a 12x12x12 dimension, which is 1,728 cubic inches. The box doesn't have to be 12x12x12; it can be 10x10x10 or long on one side as long as it's under that volume and under 5 lbs. For example, keyboards too long for Priority Mail boxes get wrapped in bubble wrap and put in a poly bag with the other items. A large Priority Mail box is 12x12x8, while a large flat rate box is 12x12x6.

knowledge.question: How do I make shipping simple for my shippers at high volume?
knowledge.answer: Levi says the less thinking a shipper has to do, the better. His shippers mainly use only large Priority Mail boxes: if a customer bought two or more items, grab a large Priority Mail box, bubble wrap and send it out. That standardization, plus free USPS boxes, is how his team ships around 1,500 units a day.

knowledge.question: Do I need a big following or lots of money to start on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says that's completely false. He started Whatnot with only two pallets in a small 150 sq ft storage unit, on his knees at a table with his laptop, not knowing anything. Six months later he had eight employees, a warehouse and a record $100,000 week. He recommends Whatnot for beginner resellers and people with zero ecom or business experience.

knowledge.question: How should I organize picking and packing orders?
knowledge.answer: Split picking and packing into separate steps. Levi's team puts each customer's order in its own box and the picker writes the lot numbers on the box in big handwriting, crossing each number out as the item goes in. Once all orders are picked, packers add tape, bubble wrap if needed, and close the box. He says dividing the two made shipping way more streamlined with far fewer errors.

knowledge.question: How do I find where a leftover item belongs after picking?
knowledge.answer: Check the back end (the CSV export) to see what happened to that number: a failed payment, a cancelled payment, or a paid item that missed its box. If it was paid, look for the boxes with numbers close to it and check which one isn't crossed out. Levi's example: item 300 was left over, and checking 229, 243 and 295 showed the box it belonged in. Because the numbers are written on the boxes, you don't have to open boxes or read labels, and they kept a 100% fulfillment rate.

knowledge.question: What do I need to ship Whatnot orders?
knowledge.answer: Levi says all you really need is a printer with 4x6 labels, 2x1 labels for your lot numbers, Wi-Fi (they use a T-Mobile Gateway), a laptop, boxes, tape and bubble wrap. He highly recommends printed 2x1 lot labels because people writing numbers by hand write 425 twice or skip numbers. They also keep 12x15 and 20x20 poly mailers for very big single items on ground shipping.

knowledge.question: What do I need to set up a streaming station?
knowledge.answer: One device to start auctions, one streaming device, two ring lights and a little more lighting, a clean comfortable table, and extra chargers for your devices. Levi says none of it has to be expensive; you can get it cheap on Temu or Amazon. That small area is all you need to get started.

knowledge.question: How should I store items so orders are easy to pick?
knowledge.answer: For electronics, Levi lines items up in number order like a bookshelf on racks on wheels, wrapped with clear shrink wrap and tape to make them more durable. For beauty, he puts 10 items in each box (10, 20, 30 and so on). He also built a mezzanine to lift spare boxes off the floor so there's room for extra racks, so they can sell 2,000 units in a day if they want.

knowledge.question: Why did Levi change single-item orders to priority mail?
knowledge.answer: Lots of people were buying one-item orders, and he wanted to use the USPS priority boxes and give faster shipping, especially during the holidays, for better reviews. All he did was change the first item from 15 oz to 16 oz, which puts single-item buyers into priority mail automatically. It's still five items for $9.21 shipping; the cost is just charged on the first item instead of split across two.

knowledge.question: Should I run my best items at the start of the show?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi doesn't recommend running all your best items upfront, because people will buy and leave. Give people a reason to stay, whether it's your personality, your talks, or special items. Tease expensive items so viewers keep an eye out, and run them randomly, which is what his team does.

knowledge.question: Is selling sports cards on Whatnot more profitable?
knowledge.answer: Levi warns it always looks greener on the other side. He spoke with someone who did $300,000 in revenue in three months selling sports cards and was negative $30,000. He also notes there aren't many sellers outside cards doing over $1 million, while his own business was on track to pass $1 million by the end of the year.

knowledge.question: Do I need a social media following to get viewers on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says Whatnot organically drives traffic to your live, and as a small seller you can see who is joining. Whatnot makes money when you make money from its fees, so the faster and more you sell, the more traffic it sends. A slow 30-second timer with a 10-second rebound won't compete with top sellers selling every 5-10 seconds.

knowledge.question: Is 5-second sudden death too fast?
knowledge.answer: Levi thinks so for most shows. Five seconds is too fast for most people to put in a custom bid, and someone who just walked in can't even process what you sold. He says many top sellers could raise profit by up to 50% just by switching to 10-second sudden death. Super-fast timers also catch first-time buyers swiping after a custom bid by accident, which he calls not really ethical and which can lead to one-star reviews and fewer returning buyers.

knowledge.question: What timer should I use as a beginner on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi doesn't recommend a 30-second timer at all; it's too slow for the algorithm, for viewers' attention spans and for resellers trying to fill their bundles. As a beginner, use at most 10+10 (10 seconds with a 10-second rebound), or at most 15 seconds sudden death. If you're doing starting bids, use 5 or 10 seconds sudden death.

knowledge.question: How should my timer change as my viewer count grows?
knowledge.answer: If you have 30-50 viewers, Levi recommends 10+10, then start lowering the timer as viewership builds. At around 80-120 viewers his team does well with 5+5, and they often use 5+7 (5 seconds required time with a 7-second counter-bid time). With 200 viewers, 10-second sudden death can work better. He knows top sellers with 300 viewers who use 20-second sudden death and get bids up to $50 because buyers have time to bid with confidence.

knowledge.question: How do I set the required time and counter-bid time on a Whatnot auction?
knowledge.answer: When you start an auction, required time options include 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 30 seconds. Levi says don't go past 15 or 20 unless you're doing sudden death. Otherwise set about 10 and a counter-bid time of 5, 7 or 10. His team uses 5+7 a lot.

knowledge.question: Should I use sudden death when I start items at $5?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says if you know you're profitable at $5, start at $5 with 10-second sudden death, which creates urgency. If three people each swipe once, you get $7 ($5, $6, $7). If you start at $1 with sudden death and three people swipe once, you only get $3. When bids are running low on a fresh shipment, his team switches from $1 starts to $3 or $5 starts.

knowledge.question: How much can a couple of extra seconds on the timer change my sale prices?
knowledge.answer: A lot, Levi says. His low-ticket beauty streams used 3-second sudden death, averaging about $5 every 3 seconds, which hit the algorithm. Switching to 5-second sudden death raised the average sale price to about $7, almost a 50% increase. He's seen shows use 2-second sudden death, which he says is too fast; that one extra second could increase profit by 100%.

knowledge.question: Does time of day affect my timer settings?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi's team goes live roughly 6:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., and around 10:00-10:30 a.m. bids start to drop. They now use 15-second sudden death instead of 10 because it gives people more time to custom bid and lets people coming in during those seconds raise the bid. They use 15-second sudden death or 5+5 on weekday mornings and go up to 5+7 when needed.

knowledge.question: How many items should I have for a 2-hour show?
knowledge.answer: Levi recommends running at least one different item per minute as a beginner, so for a 2-hour show have about 120 different items. Line them up, go in order and move quickly. If nobody swipes in 5-10 seconds, move to the next item and rerun it 10-20 minutes later. Moving fast keeps people watching because they can see 6-12 items in a minute.

knowledge.question: Should I track my own buyer data on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says data on when each customer first purchased and how often they buy is very useful, but Whatnot's analytics don't show it yet, so you have to compile your own. His team is working on that and tracks its returning buyer rate, currently 50%.

knowledge.question: Can I scale a Whatnot business by myself?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says you cannot scale Whatnot alone because you can't go live and ship every single day without burning yourself out; his operation ships roughly 400 packages a day. His top advice for any beginner is to hire a team. You don't want to be an employee in your own business; the goal is to be able to go on vacation and still make money.

knowledge.question: Is it worth hiring help if it lowers my profit margin?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi's example: doing $20,000 revenue alone might give you $4,000 profit, but hiring someone could get you to $30,000 revenue and $6,000 profit. The margin goes down, but the profit number goes up and you're doing less work, which should be the end goal.

knowledge.question: Why do people buy on Whatnot, and how does that affect which category I sell?
knowledge.answer: Levi says people buy on Whatnot for great deals and shipping. In a cheap category like health and beauty, someone who pays $3 for an item and $9.21 shipping isn't going to hop around; they'll stay to fill up their bundle. In electronics, a $50 item with $9 shipping makes the shipping a small difference, so buyers behave differently. He calls understanding this 'rule number one.'

knowledge.question: Can you really make money selling items for around $4 each?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi's beauty show averages about $4.20 per sale while buying at roughly $1 to $1.50 per unit, sometimes as low as 50 cents. If you net $1 profit per unit after cost of goods, labor, rent and everything else, and do that 30,000 times a month, that's $30,000 net profit. Many people chase $10–$20 profit per item, but volume at low prices works on Whatnot.

knowledge.question: Why is Whatnot better than Amazon for resellers?
knowledge.answer: Levi, coming from Amazon, says on Amazon you share a listing with other sellers who can drop the price penny by penny, and lowest price plus fastest shipping wins, forcing you to cut prices or hold inventory. Buyers can also return items and the seller takes the hit. On Whatnot there's no competition on your listing, you control the timer, there are no returns, and auctions bring back buyer commitment. Whatnot is also a private company focused on growing its sellers, while Amazon, eBay and Walmart keep adding fees and restrictions.

knowledge.question: Why can I invest in inventory more confidently on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says other marketplaces can pull the rug on you overnight, like Walmart shutting down its entire toy category in June, leaving sellers stuck with wholesale they can't return. On Whatnot there's less restriction and no need to unlock brands or categories, so he could buy $3.1 million in retail value within about five to six months. That confidence is a big reason he scaled so quickly.

knowledge.question: Should I buy inventory ahead of time before hiring hosts?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi's mistake in May was hiring three hosts and two shippers right away without being ahead on inventory, so he didn't have enough to run an entertaining show. On Whatnot you should be buying in advance, especially once you have employees.

knowledge.question: What kind of product mix makes a Whatnot show entertaining?
knowledge.answer: Levi says to have inventory people will buy multiples of, or that makes them stay to see what's next. For example, in his electronics show they'll sell an interesting item like a Polaroid, mixed with smaller, cheaper products like charging cups and wired or wireless headphones. Variety keeps the show entertaining.

knowledge.question: Should I show buyers how many of an item I have?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi's tip is to not show your products, because if buyers know you have many of one item, they'll spend the whole show trying to win it as cheap as possible and won't bid it up. If they believe it's your last one, they'll be more committed and swipe for it. His products rarely go over 60% of retail, so buyers still get a great deal while he maximizes profit.

knowledge.question: How often should I go live, and should I run more than one account?
knowledge.answer: Levi's team goes live almost every day, about 7 hours in the electronics show and 7 hours in the beauty show, across two accounts, with plans for three or four. He says most sellers only have one account and miss out, because multiple accounts let you test strategies other sellers can't.

knowledge.question: How do I keep my team motivated as I scale?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it's very important to clarify to your team what the goal and mission of the company is. Show them what's possible and where they can be 6 to 12 months down the road. His team knows the goal of $1 million by year end and is committed to it.

knowledge.question: Is liquidation inventory risky to sell on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says Whatnot makes it easy to invest in liquidation without losing money. If you pay 10–20% of retail, the end consumer should be willing to pay at least 30% of retail, so the worst case is you break even, move on, and find a better supplier. He spent 12 months aggressively testing suppliers and advises making educated test buys from different suppliers.

knowledge.question: How fast does money come back on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says your money comes back quickly once you hit instant early payouts, so you can reinvest much faster. He tells sellers to watch return on invested capital (ROIC), and says if you invest in a good product you can make it back in about two days on Whatnot.

knowledge.question: Why do people buy from one live seller over another?
knowledge.answer: Levi says people buy on live sales for three reasons: the streamer, the product you're holding and how your shipping works. On shipping, buyers care whether you ship fast, whether the product arrives safely, whether you offer bundle shipping and how well your bundle shipping works. All of it matters.

knowledge.question: Will my audience follow me if I start selling on a new platform?
knowledge.answer: It can, if you've built a store brand and personal brand. When Levi went live on Whatnot again, a lot of customers found them through TikTok, came to watch and comment even when not buying, and trusted them already. Buyers know the names of streamers who have been with them more than 3-4 weeks, and they quickly found one of his streamers on a brand-new Whatnot account even though he had only ever streamed on TikTok.

knowledge.question: Should a beginner buy pallets or full truckloads?
knowledge.answer: Levi recommends starting with pallets from your local liquidator. The big difference is freight: his truckloads have taken two weeks to arrive, and even pallets shipped to Delaware took about eight days. A local buyer picks up the same day with no cash tied up. Sell it on Whatnot in two or three days, get your money back, and buy another; you'll likely make more than waiting weeks for a truckload, even at a smaller margin.

knowledge.question: Why does sell-through rate matter more than margin when buying inventory?
knowledge.answer: Levi says people always chase margin and buy a truckload because the margin is higher, but forget how long it takes to sell it and how much cash is tied up. Improving your turnover and sell-through rate grows your business faster and moves the needle.

knowledge.question: How much space do I need if I buy a truckload?
knowledge.answer: Levi says if you buy a truckload you should have at least about 2,000 square feet: roughly 600 sq ft for streaming, 600 sq ft for inventory and 600 sq ft for shipping. Remember you'll still have leftover inventory on hand unless you sell the whole truckload.

knowledge.question: What should I know before buying truckloads from a liquidator?
knowledge.answer: If you buy truckloads, plan to be a consistent buyer. Levi warns that the contract holder may not give you the next truckload if someone else is buying 10 at a time, because it's hard to stand out.

knowledge.question: How does Whatnot shipping pricing work?
knowledge.answer: Levi breaks it into tiers. First-class mail is flat envelopes only and costs $0.78. Ground under 16 oz starts around $4.40 and goes up to about $8.70. From 16 oz up to 80 oz (1-5 lb) it's $9.21 no matter what the box weighs, and over 5 lb it goes ground. A Priority Mail flat rate box is also $9.21 but holds up to 70 lb.

knowledge.question: Can I put any label on any USPS box?
knowledge.answer: No. A Priority Mail label must go on a Priority Mail box, and a Priority flat rate label must go on a flat rate box. You can't put a ground label on a Priority Mail box. Levi says many people make this mistake, and the box gets sent back to you or the customer gets charged when they pick it up.

knowledge.question: What box sizes can I use for Whatnot shipping?
knowledge.answer: The $9.21 rate and ground shipping allow up to 12x12x12, which is 1,728 cubic inches. You aren't limited to that exact shape: any box under 1,728 cubic inches works, so Levi also uses longer boxes like 18x12x8. He recommends getting the large flat rate boxes and the large Priority Mail boxes.

knowledge.question: Which shipping options should I turn on in Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: In the app go to Seller Hub, then Shipping Settings (you can only do this on your phone). Set it so the buyer pays all shipping costs, and under domestic shipments turn on first-class mail, Priority Mail and USPS Ground Advantage. Don't choose Priority Mail flat rate as the default: Priority Mail can be downgraded to a flat rate box later, but flat rate is set at 12x12x6, and upgrading costs you or uses one of your five weekly label changes.

knowledge.question: Can I switch a heavy order to a flat rate box after the show?
knowledge.answer: Yes. If an order goes over 5 lb, say 10 items at 10 oz for 100 oz, but it fits in a flat rate box, you can downgrade it to a Priority flat rate box for free. It doesn't charge you or the customer more and doesn't use your weekly allowance, because they already paid the $9.21. Levi also once split a 100-backpack order into 10 boxes at no cost because the customer had already paid that shipping.

knowledge.question: How do Whatnot's built-in shipping profiles combine in a bundle?
knowledge.answer: Whatnot's profiles (0-1 oz, 1-3 oz, 4-7 oz, 8-11 oz, 12-15 oz and so on) always use the highest number behind the scenes, so 4-7 oz is actually 7 oz. They mix in a bundle: if someone buys a 15 oz bag first they might pay about $8, then a 3 oz keychain costs only the difference up to $9.21, about $1.21. Once they're between 16 and 80 oz, more items are free shipping until they hit 80 oz. If they buy the 3 oz item first, they'll pay about $4.30 for it and the bag pays the rest of the $9.21.

knowledge.question: How do I set up a custom shipping profile for 'buy two, next eight free shipping'?
knowledge.answer: Use a custom shipping profile where you choose the weight and the max per box. For beauty items averaging 8 oz, divide 80 oz by 8 to get a max of 10 per box. The first two items split the $9.21 (about $4.50 for the first), then the next eight are free shipping. That lets you say confidently on stream: buy two, next eight free shipping.

knowledge.question: How do I set up 'buy two, next three free shipping'?
knowledge.answer: Divide 80 oz by 5 to get 16 oz, but set the custom profile to 15 oz or 15.5 oz with a max of five. Don't use 16 oz, because buyers would see $9.21 on the first item, which creates buyer friction; experienced buyers see that and think something's wrong with your shipping. At 15.5 oz the first item is around $7.50-8, the second is about $1.21, and the next three are free.

knowledge.question: Do custom shipping profiles mix with each other?
knowledge.answer: Custom profiles with a max never mix, even with other custom profiles; each listing ships in its own box. Remove the max and they will mix, including with Whatnot's built-in profiles, which creates a larger box at the end. Levi recommends using a max with Priority Mail boxes to keep it simple. A max is also how one of his friends separated a consignment item he was co-hosting, so its label could be sent to the person shipping it.

knowledge.question: What shipping profile should I use during Q4?
knowledge.answer: In Q4, when USPS slows down, buyers care more about speed than cost. Levi uses Priority Mail with offers like buy one, next four free shipping, where the customer pays $9.21 upfront. One trick is a custom profile at 78 oz with a max of five, so the label says about 4.9 lb and the customer pays $9.21 no matter what. Since one item is unlikely to be heavier than 4.9 lb, you don't have to adjust labels after the show.

knowledge.question: How should I set up shipping for giveaways on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Put the giveaway in the stickers or cards category; those are the only two that allow first-class mail at $0.78. Use the 0-1 oz profile or a custom 0.1 oz profile, but never put a max on it, because a max forces 12x12x12 dimensions. Levi uses 0.1 oz so that someone who wins five giveaways still ships first-class instead of costing $4.50 in ground shipping. He says getting this right would have made him about $15,000 more in his first two months.

knowledge.question: Should I weigh every box because of Whatnot carrier adjustments?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it depends on scale. A friend doing $800,000 a month had about $15,000 in carrier adjustments, but his team of three ships 1,100 items in under 4 hours, and weighing and relabeling every box would add another 4 hours of labor. At high volume, selling and shipping more may beat relabeling. If you're smaller, you probably have time to adjust labels. As of the video, Whatnot wasn't charging the adjustments yet.

knowledge.question: Should I run big items under my regular shipping profile?
knowledge.answer: Levi thinks so. Switching profiles mid-show confuses buyers who expected free shipping in their bundle. If you run a 5 lb item under your small profile, everyone already in the free shipping range sees free shipping, so you get higher bids. Ground shipping is cheap between about 6 and 20 lb, so you might eat about $4. Run big items in the middle or toward the end when there are still a lot of people in the show, then unbundle after.

knowledge.question: What kinds of products are easiest to ship on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi tries to keep items small, like keychains, small mouses, pins and beauty items. Box size is hard to calculate with random pulls at volume, which is part of why Whatnot hasn't charged for box-size adjustments; a large game board that weighs 2 lb can go bigger than 12x12x12. Small items avoid that problem.

knowledge.question: What is the Whatnot Rewards Club and how does it help viewership?
knowledge.answer: Every 3 months, Whatnot lets you offer tiered incentives (bronze, silver, gold, platinum and diamond) to get customers to buy more. The big benefit is notifications: once someone is in a tier, Whatnot keeps sending them pulses like 'you have unused coupons' and 'this person is live now.' Levi says notifications are how you drive people to click on your live, so every member in your Rewards Club is someone getting pulled back to your show.

knowledge.question: How hard should I make the Rewards Club tiers?
knowledge.answer: Make the bronze tier easy to hit. Levi made it harder to reach each tier last season and made coupons less valuable, and his members dropped from 2,000 to 1,000. That's a thousand people not getting notified, which he believes hurt his viewership. His new plan: make the first three tiers easy, tiers four and five a little harder, and make the coupons more attractive.

knowledge.question: Should my Rewards Club coupons be a percentage or a dollar amount?
knowledge.answer: Levi recommends a dollar amount based on your average sale price. A percentage coupon applies to any purchase, so if you sell high-ticket items, 20% off a $400 item is an $80 discount. He sells everything from $2 to $3 items and $6 average beauty items up to $300 to $400 items, so a percentage would be too risky. Also think about whether you'll sell the same inventory for 90 days or mix in new products.

knowledge.question: Can resellers abuse my Rewards Club coupons?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Resellers are allowed to make new accounts, and some will make several just to rank up and collect coupons again. Levi has had a customer use two accounts back when he sold a lot of electronics. Since you're locked in for the 90-day season and can't change it until it's over, don't make every tier too easy and the coupon value too high, or it can become a big discount.
